title.en: Poem: For Anne Gregory (W. B. Yeats)
Yellow hair or the person inside?

text.en: If everyone admires you only for your striking looks, how do you know anyone truly loves you for who you are? W. B. Yeats turns that question into a crisp three-stanza conversation.

For Anne Gregory by W. B. Yeats is a three-stanza musical conversation between an older speaker (perhaps the poet) and a young woman with bright honey-coloured hair, Anne Gregory.
In Stanza 1, the speaker warns gently that young men thrown into despair by those 'great honey-coloured ramparts at your ear' may love her only for her golden hair, not 'you alone'. Notice 'ramparts' (fortress walls) as a metaphor for curls framing her face.
In Stanza 2, Anne responds cleverly: she can easily get a hair-dye and turn her yellow hair brown, black, or carrot-red—so that young men will look past surface colour and love her 'for myself alone'.
In Stanza 3, the speaker replies thoughtfully with something he heard 'yesternight': an old religious man declared he had found a text proving that only God could love human beings solely for their inner self, never for their yellow hair.
Yeats blends playful wit with tenderness: while humans are naturally drawn by appearance, true spiritual love values the unseen soul within—and we too should try to look beyond outer looks.

caption.en: Trace imagery, tone and central idea

text.en: For Anne Gregory by W. B. Yeats is structured like a friendly three-stanza dialogue about outer looks versus inner character.
In Stanza 1, the speaker addresses Anne Gregory directly about the admirers drawn to her appearance.
He describes her thick golden curls as 'great honey-coloured ramparts at your ear'.
What are ramparts? High protective stone walls around a fort—here comparing hair framing her face to fortress walls protecting her true self.
He doubts that any young man loves her strictly for herself alone, rather than merely her bright yellow hair.
Stanza 2 belongs to Anne Gregory's spirited reply, wrapped in quotation marks.
She points out that outer looks are temporary and controllable: she can easily buy hair dye and change her yellow hair.
Notice the vivid colour list—brown, black, or carrot—chosen to prove appearance shouldn't dictate love.
Anne hopes that without striking golden hair, suitors will learn to value her for herself alone.
In Stanza 3, the speaker shares what an old religious man told him 'yesternight' from a sacred text.
The old man concluded that only God is completely free of surface bias and capable of loving a person purely for their inner soul.
Does this mean human love is worthless? No—Yeats wryly reminds us that mortals naturally notice beauty, yet true depth requires looking deeper.
Look at the stanza rhyme pattern: abcbdb, keeping a gentle song-like cadence across each six-line stanza.
The poem leaves students with a clear reflection: physical charm fades or changes, while inner character defines who we truly are.

problem.en: Explain the metaphor 'honey-coloured ramparts at your ear' and why Anne mentions brown, black, or carrot hair.

text.en: Ramparts are fort walls; Yeats uses this metaphor for heavy golden curls shielding Anne's face.

why.en: Suggests outer beauty attracts attention yet hides the real person within.

text.en: Anne suggests dyeing her hair brown, black, or carrot to test true affection.

why.en: Shows surface colour is changeable and trivial compared to identity.

text.en: The religious man's text contrasts imperfect mortal eyes with unconditional divine love.

why.en: Reinforces valuing inner goodness over fleeting looks.

prompt.en: How does Yeats contrast human attraction with God's love in For Anne Gregory, and why is Anne willing to dye her hair?

requiredIdeas.en: Young men risk loving Anne primarily for her honey-coloured hair ('ramparts')
Anne offers to dye her hair brown, black, or carrot so admirers love her for herself
An old religious man's text says only God loves purely for the inner self, not yellow hair

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking Anne dislikes hair colour rather than wanting love based on character

points.en: Yeats frames For Anne Gregory as a three-stanza conversation about beauty vs inner identity.
Her golden curls are called 'honey-coloured ramparts', attractive yet hiding the true person.
Anne wants to dye her hair brown, black, or carrot so people love her for who she is inside.
According to the old religious man's text, only God loves people purely for themselves alone, never for yellow hair.
